Subject: Provisional slab sizing & surge mitigation — quick data request

Hi Lisa —

Thanks again for the call this morning. Per our conversation, I want to start drafting a provisional dedicated slab recommendation so Procurement and Engineering at Skyward have numbers to evaluate. To make that recommendation concrete we need a couple of inputs from your side (I put the minimum we need below). If you can share the Excel load file you mentioned (or confirm the bullets), we’ll run a short scenario model and return a slab sizing + burst policy you can review.

What we need from Skyward:
- Typical request profile: median and 95th percentile request tokens (prompt+response) — e.g., median 80 tokens, p95 240 tokens
- Average requests per minute during normal hours and peak-hour concurrent requests (not daily totals alone)
- Expected launch-day peak (if any) and planned marketing spikes (dates)
- Target p95 latency SLO for generation (millisecond target) and acceptable % of overflow to hosted fallback
- Preferred model family for production (your team mentioned a lightweight 13B quantized variant)

A few notes on how we model:
- We convert your per-request token distribution into tokens/sec demand at peak concurrency, then map tokens/sec to GPU count for the chosen model profile.
- We size the dedicated slab to meet your p95 latency SLO at peak + a headroom buffer (we typically recommend 30–50% headroom depending on traffic burstiness).
- For contract proposals we include a baseline commit and a burst/overage plan (burst typically handled by a mix of dedicated spare capacity + hosted fallback on an approximate smaller model).

If you prefer, feel free to drop the Skyward_MLP_Loads.xlsx file in a shared Drive link and we’ll take it from there. I’ll loop Jordan and Priyom on the analysis.

Thanks —

From: Jordan Blake <jordan_blake@redwood.com>
To: Mina Haddad <mina@redwood.com>, Priyom Das <priyom_das@redwood.com>
Date: Fri, 24 May 2024 10:28:00 -0700
Subject: RE: Provisional slab sizing & surge mitigation — quick data request

Mina / Priyom —

I ran a quick back-of-envelope using the numbers Lisa provided. I’ll put the assumptions up front and then give three scenarios (Conservative / Recommended / Aggressive). These are provisional — Priyom, feel free to correct kernel-level perf numbers.

Assumptions:
- Model: redwood-13b-q4 (production quantized 13B) running on A100-style 40GB GPU
- Avg generation throughput per GPU (steady-state, optimized batching & KV cache): ~420 tokens/sec (this is conservative for q4 with 4-bit kernels and continuous batching for typical 120–256 token generation windows)
- Effective tokens per request at p95: 280 tokens (from Skyward)
- Peak concurrent active requests: 110 (observed), but marketing spike could create 3x that for short windows

Mapping formula: GPUs needed = ceil( (concurrent_requests * avg_tokens_per_request) / (gpu_tokens_per_sec * target_seconds_per_request_window) ). For our quick calc we use the instantaneous tokens/sec demand formula: tokens/sec_demand = concurrent_requests * (tokens_per_request / avg_response_time_seconds). To meet p95 latency target we budget response time <= SLO.

Scenarios:
1) Conservative (SLO envelope tight; 50% headroom)
- Target p95 = 250 ms (Skyward prefers better for clinical flows)
- Tokens/sec demand (baseline peak 110 concurrent): tokens/sec = 110 * (280 tokens / 0.25 s) = 123,200 tokens/sec
- GPUs required = ceil(123,200 / 420) = 294 GPUs -> clearly not practical, so we must change the model for low-latency flows or shard differently.

2) Recommended (mix of dedicated + fallback smaller-model streaming; 40% headroom)
- Target p95 = 350 ms (company-wide SLO)
- tokens/sec = 110 * (280 / 0.35) = 88,000 tokens/sec
- GPUs = ceil(88,000 / 420) = 210 GPUs.
- Practical proposal: provision a modest dedicated slab sized to handle steady peak of core users (choose 6–12 GPUs) combined with a burst policy: Redwood Dedicated slab (A100x6) as committed capacity for deterministic throughput on critical flows; overflow routed to Redwood Hosted pool where a smaller quantized 7B (or multi-variant routing) can handle the majority of burst traffic with graceful degradation.
- Headroom: configured autoscaling + reserved burst tokens in the contract to cover expected marketing spikes; we recommend budgeting ~40% additional hosted capacity to handle expected 3x marketing spikes for short windows.

3) Aggressive (full on-prem style coverage; higher commit)
- If Skyward wants dedicated-only handling of 3x marketing spikes without fallback, the compute numbers scale linearly; for a 3x instantaneous concurrency (330), tokens/sec = 330*(280/0.35)= 264,000 -> GPUs ~ 629. This is an enterprise-only footprint and would be priced accordingly.

Comments:
- The raw GPU counts above show why we typically recommend a hybrid approach: dedicated slab to guarantee low-latency for critical paths + hosted fallback (smaller model or degraded mode) for broad burst coverage.
- For specific endpoints where p95 must be ~250 ms we should propose pinning those requests to a dedicated micro-slab (e.g., 2–4 GPUs) and using more aggressive batching and cache pre-warm strategies.

Priyom — can you run a quick perf table for redwood-13b-q4 and redwood-7b-q4 on an A100 and a T4 so we can quantify hosted fallback delta and refine the slab recommendation?

— Jordan

Subject: RE: Provisional slab sizing & surge mitigation — consolidated recommendation and next steps

Tom / Lisa —

Appreciate the procurement checklist. Below is a consolidated, pragmatic recommendation that balances your latency objectives and realistic GPU economics. This is a provisional proposal we can put into the MAP and commercial proposal.

Executive summary (one-paragraph):
We recommend a hybrid committed slab approach: dedicate a 6-GPU A100 slab to guarantee deterministic low-latency for critical clinical flows (p95 target ~250 ms for pinned endpoints). For broader product traffic, use Redwood Hosted overflow with a quantized 7B fallback model that accepts slightly higher latency (p95 ~450 ms) during marketing spikes. Contractually: baseline commit = A100x6 + X reserved burst token pool; we include a documented autoscale and fallback policy and SOC2 evidence bundle for procurement.

Detailed sizing rationale:
- Dedicated slab: A100 x6. Why: with conservative batching and priority routing this slab will absorb steady peak requests from critical endpoints and provide consistent p95 performance. Operationally we pin the most latency-sensitive endpoints (clinical summaries) to the slab so their p95 sits comfortably under 300 ms.
- Headroom: configure runtime autoscale guardrails + reserved hosted burst capacity equal to ~40% of expected peak token/sec demand to cover short 2–3x spikes for up to 2 hours.
- Fallback routing: non-critical endpoints will be routed to hosted pool using redwood-7b-q4 during overflow; we will document degradation modes and callback behavior.
- Observability: Console dashboards will expose token-level cost, route-level latency, and cache-warm metrics so Skyward can validate when fallback is used.

Procurement / SLA notes:
- Latency SLA (for dedicated-pinned endpoints): Redwood will commit to an operational objective of p95 < 300 ms on the pinned dedicated slab; SLA credits can be discussed if sustained deviations occur due to operator error.
- For overflow-hosted traffic we do not guarantee the same p95; we will include an explicit fallback policy in the MAP that enumerates acceptable degraded bounds and reroute thresholds.
- SOC2: we will provide our SOC2 Type II report and a KMS integration summary in the procurement bundle.

Next steps / asks for Skyward:
1) Confirm which endpoints are pinned (list). We recommend initially pinning up to 3 critical flows.
2) Approve the MAP timeline or propose edits to MAP_Skyward_Rev1.docx.
3) Accept the commercial stub: A100x6 baseline commit + hosted burst pool with overage pricing to be supplied by Jordan in a separate commercial sheet.

I’ll coordinate with Jordan on the commercial sheet and Priyom on perf numbers. If it helps, we can schedule a 30-minute sizing review next week and walk through the numbers and fallback flows.

Best —
